title: Pre-Placement Maltreatment as the Primary Driver of Adult Psychiatric Risk: How Foster Care Quality Modulates, Compounds, or Repairs Early Adversity
content: Adults who spent childhood in foster care carry among the highest burdens of psychiatric illness in the American population, yet the sources of that burden remain contested. One influential account attributes adult mental illness to the maltreatment that precedes placement: abuse, neglect, and household dysfunction that accumulate before state intervention. A competing account emphasizes features of the placement experience itself — removal from family, placement instability, and systemic failures in service delivery. This narrative review synthesizes four decades of evidence, including landmark adverse childhood experiences studies, prospective birth-cohort and administrative-record designs, twin–co-twin analyses, quasi-experimental meta-analyses, and the only randomized controlled trial of foster care (the Bucharest Early Intervention Project). The weight of evidence indicates that pre-placement adversity is the dominant driver of adult psychiatric risk, operating through well-characterized dose–response and neurobiological pathways; however, placement-related factors — particularly caregiver disruption and instability, inequitable kinship versus non-kinship placement patterns, and acute mental health service discontinuities at aging out — exert independent, modifiable effects. We conclude that a bifurcated framing mischaracterizes the evidence: pre-placement adversity sets the psychiatric baseline, and the quality of out-of-home care determines whether that trajectory is compounded or partially repaired. Prevention of maltreatment, minimization of unnecessary removal, rapid stabilization in care, and seamless service continuity constitute the highest-yield policy targets.
